title: Building Chaturbrah: LiveKit, WebRTC, and Real-Time Streaming
content:
Recently I was approached about a role working on a large-scale video streaming platform.

The tech stack and problem space were interesting - things like low-latency video, real-time interaction, and performance at scale. It's not something I've had direct professional experience with, so instead of just reading about it, I decided to build something.

That's where **Chaturbrah** came from - a place to chat with ur brahs.

The goal was simple: get hands-on experience with real-time streaming concepts and build something that actually works end-to-end.

## What It Does

Chaturbrah is a lightweight live streaming app where:

- A user can go live with their camera and microphone
- Other users can join and watch in real time
- Everyone in the stream can chat
- The homepage shows who is currently live and how many viewers they have

There's no real account system yet. Users pick a username locally, and that becomes their identity.

Each streamer has their own stream page, and viewers can jump directly into any live stream from the homepage.

## Why LiveKit (and not raw WebRTC)

When you start looking into streaming, everything eventually leads to WebRTC.

WebRTC is what actually powers real-time video and audio in the browser, but building directly on top of it is not trivial. You're dealing with signaling, peer connections, ICE candidates, NAT traversal, scaling, and a lot of low-level details that don't really help you learn product-level streaming concepts quickly.

I didn't want to spend weeks just getting a basic connection working.

Instead, I used **LiveKit**.

LiveKit sits on top of WebRTC and handles the hard infrastructure problems:

- Peer connection management
- Media routing and transport
- Scaling across multiple participants
- Data channels for real-time messaging

That let me focus on how a streaming product actually behaves, instead of getting stuck in protocol-level details.

## How It Works

- **Frontend**: React + TypeScript + Vite + Tailwind (Vercel)
- **Backend**: Node + Express (Render)
- **Realtime Media + Data**: LiveKit Cloud

The backend is responsible for generating short-lived tokens that allow clients to connect to LiveKit rooms with specific permissions.

From there, everything happens in the browser.

Each stream is just a LiveKit room named after the streamer's username.

- Broadcasters connect and publish their camera and microphone
- Viewers connect and subscribe to those tracks
- Chat and latency pings are sent over LiveKit data channels

There's no separate WebSocket server and no database. Everything is real-time and ephemeral.

When a streamer goes live, the backend registers that stream in memory. The frontend polls for active streams and renders them on the homepage with viewer counts.

## Some Interesting Challenges

### Getting "Live" Right

At first, a viewer could connect to a room and immediately see a "Live" badge, even if no one was actually streaming.

The fix was to tie the live state to whether a remote video track is present, not just whether the connection exists.

It's a small detail, but it makes a big difference in how the app feels.

### Handling Multi-Tab and Strict Mode

React Strict Mode caused effects to run twice in development, which led to multiple connections to the same room.

That resulted in inflated viewer counts and duplicate behavior.

Adding guards to ensure a single connection fixed the issue.

### Preventing Multiple Broadcasters

Each stream is tied to a username, so I needed to prevent multiple users from going live under the same name.

The backend keeps a simple in-memory registry of active streams and blocks duplicate broadcasters for that username.

### Real-Time Chat Without a Chat Server

Instead of building a separate WebSocket service, chat runs over LiveKit's data channels.

Messages are sent alongside the media connection, which keeps the architecture simple and tightly integrated.

### Thumbnail Previews

For the homepage, each live stream shows a preview image.

Instead of storing thumbnails, the app briefly connects as a "preview" client, captures a single video frame, and disconnects.

It's lightweight and makes the directory feel much more dynamic.

## Looking Back (and Ahead)

This started as a way to get familiar with streaming concepts, but it ended up turning into a small, fully functional product.

There are still a lot of directions to take it:

- A real account system instead of local usernames
- Persistent chat and stream history
- Better discovery and filtering
- Moderation tools
- More advanced player features

The biggest takeaway was understanding how the pieces fit together.

WebRTC is doing the real work under the hood, but using something like LiveKit makes it possible to focus on the actual user experience - how streams are presented, how users interact, and how everything behaves in real time.

Chaturbrah isn't trying to be a full streaming platform. It's a focused way to explore how one works, and to build something real instead of just talking about it.

title: Building SignalChain: Email Triage and Logistics Signals
content:
I was recently interviewing with a company whose product deals with a problem I thought was genuinely interesting: taking messy operational communication and turning it into something structured and useful.

A lot of important updates do not arrive as neat records in a system. They show up in emails. A vendor mentions a delay. A warehouse appointment changes. A shipment is held up. A revised ETA is buried in a paragraph. Sometimes the message matters. Sometimes it does not. Sometimes it is not even related to operations at all.

That problem stuck with me, so I decided to build a small prototype around it.

That prototype became **SignalChain**.

## What SignalChain Does

SignalChain is a simple workflow app built around one idea: pull in inbox messages, identify which ones look operationally relevant, and turn those messages into something more structured than raw email text.

Right now, it can:

- connect to a Gmail inbox
- load recent messages
- group them into likely relevant vs other
- open a selected email
- analyze the message with OpenAI
- classify unrelated messages safely
- return a structured result with key details, business impact, and recommended actions

The goal was not to build a full logistics platform. The goal was to build a believable slice of one.

## Why I Built It

What interested me was not just the AI part.

The interesting part was the workflow around it.

How should the inbox be grouped? What kinds of messages should be surfaced first? What happens when the message is clearly not relevant? How do you present extracted information in a way that feels useful instead of just dumping model output into a box?

That felt like a good product and frontend exercise, not just an API integration exercise.

## Under the Hood

SignalChain is a fullstack TypeScript app built as a monorepo.

**Frontend:** React, Vite, TypeScript, Tailwind  
**Backend:** Node, Express, TypeScript

There are two main integrations in the current version:

**Gmail**  
I wired up a Gmail OAuth flow so the app can connect to an inbox and load recent email messages.

**OpenAI**  
When a message is analyzed, the backend sends the email subject and body through an extraction step powered by OpenAI. The result is normalized into a structured shape for the UI.

That output currently includes things like:

- whether the message is logistics-related
- issue type
- summary
- business impact
- key details
- recommended actions

## What Turned Out to Matter

One of the first things I ran into was that inboxes are noisy.

The app could not just assume every message was relevant. Security alerts, password resets, promos, and random non-operational emails all needed to be handled cleanly. That meant the inbox experience itself mattered, not just the analysis step.

So part of the project became about:

- grouping messages more intelligently
- making sure irrelevant emails do not get treated like shipment issues
- keeping recommendations concise instead of overly verbose
- making the UI feel like a workflow tool instead of an AI demo

That turned out to be the most interesting part of the build.

## Where It Is Now

At this point, SignalChain is in a pretty solid prototype state.

It can connect to a real inbox, pull in messages, classify them, and generate structured analysis in the UI. It is not pretending to be a complete product, but it is enough to explore the shape of one.

## What I’d Explore Next

There are a lot of directions this could go from here.

A more complete version would probably need to go beyond the email body alone. In real operations workflows, the important information may be in:

- attachments
- PDFs
- spreadsheets
- chat systems like Slack
- other system-generated updates

I would also want to keep improving the workflow side of the product - better prioritization, better triage, better refresh behavior, and cleaner ways to move from "this message matters" to "here is what to do next."

That is the part I find most interesting: not just extracting information, but building software that helps reduce the amount of noise a person has to sort through.

title: Thunder Funk: Lo-Fi Weather Vibes
content:
About a year ago, I built **Thunder Funk**, a lo-fi, cyberpunk-style weather app. The idea was simple - take something boring like checking the weather and make it feel like a whole vibe.

Recently I started reading *Neuromancer* by William Gibson, and that aesthetic pulled me right back into this project.

Thunder Funk turns the weather into a scene. You get a city through a window, subtle motion from rain or snow, a cat on the sill, neon UI layered over the glass, and a track that matches what it feels like outside.

It’s less about raw data and more about the mood.

---

## How It Works

- **Frontend**: React + TypeScript + Tailwind (Vercel)
- **Backend**: Rails API (Render)
- No database - everything is fetched live and mapped in code

The backend acts as a wrapper around the WeatherAPI service, handling requests and returning normalized data to the frontend.

There’s also caching in place using Redis, so repeated requests for the same location don’t constantly hit the external API. That keeps things fast and avoids unnecessary calls.

From there, the frontend maps conditions to a track + visual effect, and the scene updates accordingly.

---

## Looking Back (and Ahead)

This was fully built about a year ago, but I never wrote about it. Coming back to it now, there are a few things I’d want to clean up.

The biggest one is music. Right now it’s just YouTube embeds, which works, but isn’t great. Browser autoplay rules make it awkward, so it ends up feeling more like "click to start" than something seamless.

If I revisit it, I’d probably:

- Swap YouTube for a real audio player
- Trigger playback after first interaction so it behaves consistently
- Improve the track selection
- Add more polish to the visuals

---

Thunder Funk isn’t trying to be the best weather app. It’s just trying to make checking the weather a little more fun.

title: Building MoodStack: My First Real Dive into AWS
content:
I recently had an interview where we ended up talking about real-world IoT systems – how devices could send frequent updates (like coffee machines broadcasting when they're done brewing or the amount of coffee they have left) and how you might handle that kind of architecture. I didn't have access to actual hardware, so I started thinking: how could I simulate a similar system with cloud services?

That's where **MoodStack** was born.

I wanted to build something small but functional that gave me a chance to work with AWS tools. Something event-driven with real-time updates, and ideally, a little fun to use. What I came up with is a game-like app where you interact with a group of NPCs and influence their mood, either for good or for chaos.

---

## What MoodStack Does

MoodStack is a mini-experiment in real-time state management using serverless tools. You pick a role – Caretaker or Chaos Agent – and perform actions like "Give Hug" or "Trip." Each action changes the NPC's mood, which is instantly reflected in the UI.

Behind the scenes, these actions are sent through an API and recorded in a database, and WebSocket messages make sure everyone else sees those mood changes live.

---

## How It Works (Under the Hood)

- **Frontend**: Built with React + Vite + TypeScript and styled with Tailwind.
- **API Gateway**: Handles incoming REST requests and WebSocket connections.
- **Lambda Functions**: Core logic lives here – handling mood updates, state reads, and event history.
- **DynamoDB**: Stores current mood state and mood event history for each NPC.
- **WebSockets**: Broadcast mood updates so all clients stay in sync in real time.

The frontend also uses **optimistic UI updates** – when you take an action, the score floats up and the mood updates immediately, before waiting for confirmation from the backend. Once the real update comes back via WebSocket, the app reconciles it.

---

## Hosting and Deployment

I went full AWS for hosting:

- **Amplify** handles frontend builds and deployment. I connected it to my GitHub repo so every push to `main` triggers a new deploy to an S3 bucket behind a CloudFront CDN.
- **Route 53** manages DNS, pointing my custom subdomain (e.g. `moodstack.thisdev.rocks`) to the Amplify app.
- **Certificate Manager** handles SSL, all provisioned automatically through Amplify.

This setup means the whole thing is serverless, scalable, and very hands-off once deployed.

---

## What's Next

I've got a few more ideas I'd like to explore:

- SQS to decouple write-heavy traffic and simulate burst handling
- Game mode with coins, scoring, and competition (team-based or 1v1)
- Auth to restrict API access
- More polish on layout, animations, and accessibility
- Maybe even actual device integration someday, to tie it back to those original IoT thoughts

---

MoodStack started as a way to get my hands dirty with AWS, but it's turning into a surprisingly fun platform to build on. I'll be adding more features and tweaks over time, so stay tuned for updates.
